Maryland property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Owners may appeal the total new market value within 45 days from the date on the assessment notice. (SDAT: Questions and Answers About Real Property Assessments; source)
  • Appeals may be filed upon receipt of an assessment notice, by a petition for review, and upon purchase of property between January 1 and June 30. (SDAT: Assessment Appeal Process; source)
  • Property is reassessed every 3 years, and the assessment increase is phased in equally over three years. (SDAT: Questions and Answers About Real Property Assessments; source)
  • After the Supervisor's level hearing, a further appeal to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board must be filed within 30 days of the final notice. (SDAT: Assessment Appeal Process; source)
  • An appeal of a Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board decision goes to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the PTAAB order; the owner must be present (no written hearings). (SDAT: Assessment Appeal Process; source)
  • At a tax sale the county's tax lien certificate is sold at public auction to the highest bidder; the homeowner still owns the property. (SDAT: Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman; source)
  • Thirty days or more before first advertisement, the Collector must mail a notice to the last-appearing owner. (SDAT: Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman; source)

Maryland offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • The Homestead Tax Credit limits the assessment increase on which tax is paid on the owner's principal residence; it is calculated on increases above the 10% State limit (or a lower local cap). (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • The credit applies only when the annual assessment increase exceeds 10%. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners must submit a one-time application to establish eligibility for the credit. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • The dwelling must be the owner's principal residence, lived in at least six months of the year including July 1; one property only; credit requires the property was not transferred to new ownership. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit (income-based): combined gross household income cannot exceed $60,000 and net worth (excluding the home and retirement accounts) must be under $200,000. (SDAT: Homeowners' Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit application deadline is October 1 each year; apply by April 15 to have the credit on the tax bill; apply at least 30 days before settlement to receive credit at settlement. (SDAT: Homeowners' Property Tax Credit Program; source)

Maryland evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • Before filing a failure-to-pay-rent case, the landlord must give written notice of intent (form DC-CV-115) stating rent due and giving 10 days to pay. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • Failure-to-pay-rent cases are filed in District Court in the county where the property is located (form DC-CV-082). (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • After judgment for possession in a failure-to-pay-rent case, eviction cannot start until 7 business days have passed. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • Breach-of-lease and tenant-holding-over cases allow eviction to be sought immediately after judgment. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • The landlord requests a Warrant of Restitution within 60 days of judgment (failure to pay rent) and must notify the tenant of the eviction date at least 6 days before. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • Landlord must give written notice of intent to terminate a tenancy: 60 days for a written lease for a stated term (over 1 week) or month-to-month tenancy. (Real Property Art. 8-402(c); source)
  • Year-to-year tenancies require 90 days' notice; week-to-week tenancies 7 days (written lease) or 21 days (no written lease). (Real Property Art. 8-402(c); source)
  • If the landlord receives a notice of intent to foreclose, notice to end tenancy is at least 30 days (month-to-month/week-to-week) or 60 days (year-to-year). (Real Property Art. 8-402(c); source)
  • A foreclosure sale may not occur until at least 45 days after service of process when the property is not owner-occupied. (Real Property Art. 7-105.1(n); source)

What the official sources say

  • A TOD deed is effective if recorded in the land records of the property's county before the transferor's death. (HB 738 (2026), Estates & Trusts Art.; source)
  • A TOD deed is effective without notice, delivery or acceptance by the beneficiary during the transferor's life, and without consideration. (HB 738 (2026), Estates & Trusts Art.; source)
  • The transferor may revoke a recorded TOD deed by recording an executed and acknowledged revocation before death. (HB 738 (2026), Estates & Trusts Art.; source)
  • The Act applies to a TOD deed made before, on, or after its effective date if the transferor dies on or after that date. (HB 738 (2026); source)

Maryland Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Maryland rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Maryland?

It is a deed that names who gets a house when the owner dies, signed and recorded while the owner is alive. Maryland's version took effect October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738, Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws.

The new subtitle sits in Real Property Article 14-1001 and following. The owner stays in control for life: the deed gives the named beneficiary no ownership until death. The Daily Record's October 2026 explainer compares it to a beneficiary designation on a bank account or life insurance policy.

The Act applies to a deed made before, on or after October 1, 2026, if the owner dies on or after that date. The Daily Record advises talking with an estate planning attorney about drafting and recording, and about how the deed fits with a will and the rest of the plan.

  • Owner: called the transferor in the statute.
  • Beneficiary: the person or people named to receive the property.
  • Joint owners: owners with survivorship rights, such as tenants by the entirety, are treated differently from tenants in common.

Who can sign one and what must it say?

Any owner with the capacity needed to make a will can sign one. The deed must follow the execution rules in Estates and Trusts 4-101 and must state that the transfer to the beneficiary happens at the owner's death.

The statutory form in 14-1011 includes owner and beneficiary information, a legal description, the transfer-at-death statement, and preparer and notary sections. Its notes say witnesses and notaries cannot be relatives of the owners or beneficiaries, or beneficiaries themselves.

A deed can name one beneficiary or several. If it names several and does not say how they hold title, they take as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. A deed can also name alternate beneficiaries, including successive alternates, who take if a primary beneficiary does not survive the owner.

How is a Maryland TOD deed recorded and taxed?

It must be recorded in the land records of the county where the house sits before the owner dies, or it has no effect. Signing it is not enough.

Recording follows Real Property 3-104 with several changes the Act makes for TOD deeds. The collector's endorsement, certain intake sheet and assessment office endorsements, and the attorney or party preparation certification do not apply. The clerk may still refuse a TOD deed that comes without an intake sheet. The assessment records do not change to the beneficiary's name until the owner's death.

ItemRule under Chapter 751
When it takes effectAt the owner's death, if recorded before then
Notice to beneficiaryNot required during the owner's life
ConsiderationNot required
State recordation tax and state and county transfer taxExempt if primary or secondary residence of the owner
Inheritance taxBeneficiaries may still owe it, per the form's informational sheet

The enrolled bill cites Tax-Property 12-108, 13-207 and 13-414 for these exemptions.

What can the owner still do while alive?

Almost everything. The deed does not change the owner's right to live in, sell or mortgage the house, and it does not give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.

Section 14-1007 lists what a recorded TOD deed does not do during the owner's life.

  • It does not limit the owner's right to sell or encumber the property.
  • It does not affect a buyer's or lender's rights, even if they know about the deed.
  • It does not affect the rights of the owner's creditors, including future ones.
  • It does not affect eligibility for public assistance, including Medicaid, for the owner or the beneficiary.
  • It does not expose the house to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

The Daily Record notes this is a difference from adding a relative to the title as a joint owner, which can expose the house to that person's creditors, lawsuits or divorce and gives them present rights.

How is a TOD deed changed or revoked?

By recording a new document before the owner dies. A TOD deed is always revocable, even if the deed itself says otherwise.

There are three ways to revoke all or part of a recorded deed, each recorded in the county land records.

  • A new TOD deed that expressly revokes the earlier one or conflicts with it.
  • An instrument of revocation that says so expressly.
  • A lifetime deed that expressly revokes the TOD deed.

A will cannot revoke a recorded TOD deed, and neither can marking up the deed itself. With joint owners, a deed is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke. The statutory form notes that a TOD deed naming a spouse is revoked automatically by divorce or annulment, and that it is also revoked if the owner later marries and has a child by birth, adoption or legitimation.

What happens when the owner dies?

Title passes to the surviving beneficiary by operation of law, without probate for that house. The beneficiary takes subject to any existing mortgage, lien, security interest or encumbrance, and the transfer carries no warranty of title.

If a beneficiary does not survive the owner, that share lapses, and an alternate takes if one is named. A beneficiary who intentionally killed the owner is disqualified, and the Act keeps the rights of pretermitted children and the elective share of a spouse in play. Any beneficiary may disclaim, and for real property the disclaimer must be recorded in the county land records.

Section 14-1013 creates an optional Notification of Death form. The statute sets no deadline to record it, and the transfer happens at death whether or not it is recorded. Recording it still matters, because the clerk forwards it to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation so the property records can be updated. If a beneficiary who lives in the house uses the form's occupancy option, the beneficiary certifies under penalty of perjury to live there as a principal residence for at least 7 of the next 12 months.

How does a TOD deed affect selling the house?

The owner can sell the house any time while alive without the beneficiary's consent. After death, the beneficiary can sell once title has passed and the paperwork is in order.

A beneficiary who inherits through a TOD deed takes a house with whatever debt is attached. A buyer or title company may ask to see the recorded TOD deed and the notification of death, if one was recorded.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including inherited homes. If you are a beneficiary and the house needs repairs or has back taxes, call us before you spend money on repairs. If you are an owner thinking about a TOD deed and a sale, remember that the deed does not stop you from selling while you are alive.

The Daily Record lists tax effects, existing liens, multiple beneficiaries, possible family disputes and Medicaid or long-term care planning among the points to check before relying on a TOD deed.

More questions about Maryland Transfer on Death Deed

When did Maryland's transfer on death deed take effect?

October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738 (Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws). It covers deeds made before, on or after that date if the owner dies on or after it.

Does a TOD deed have to be recorded?

Yes. It is effective only if recorded in the land records of the county where the property is located before the owner's death.

Can I still sell my house if I record a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed does not limit your right to sell or mortgage the property, and it does not give the beneficiary any interest while you are alive.

Does a will override a TOD deed in Maryland?

No. A recorded TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will. It can be revoked by a recorded new TOD deed, a recorded revocation, or a recorded lifetime deed.

Does a TOD deed avoid inheritance tax?

No. The recordation and transfer taxes are exempt for a residence, but beneficiaries may still owe inheritance tax, according to the informational sheet with the form.

content:
Maryland Closing Costs for Sellers: Transfer Tax, Recording and What You Pay

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maryland Closing Costs for Sellers sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Recordation and State/local transfer taxes are presumed split equally between buyer and seller absent a contrary agreement. (Real Property Art. 14-104; source)
  • Nonresident individual sellers must pay 8.75% of the total sale payment as withholding; nonresident entities 8.25%, via Form MW506NRS at settlement. (Comptroller: Employer Withholding; source)
  • A county or municipality may charge up to $55 for a certificate of paid charges in certain counties. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What taxes make up Maryland seller closing costs?

Three government charges drive most Maryland closing statements: the State transfer tax, a county transfer tax and a recordation tax. The State transfer tax is 0.5% of the consideration, and the county taxes vary by county.

These are charges on the deed, so they appear whether or not a real estate agent is involved. A recording fee and a surcharge are added by the Clerk of the Circuit Court, and the property tax account has to be clear before the deed is accepted.

  • State transfer tax: 0.5% of consideration, collected by the Circuit Court clerk.
  • County transfer tax: set by each county, from 0% to 1.5% in the Department of Legislative Services table.
  • Recordation tax: set by each county per $500 of consideration.
  • Recording fee and surcharge: charged by the clerk for each instrument.
  • Property tax and other county charges due: paid before the transfer is entered.

Who pays the transfer and recordation taxes in Maryland?

Under Real Property Article 14-104, recordation tax and the State and local transfer taxes are presumed to be shared equally between buyer and seller unless the contract or the law says otherwise. Most Maryland contracts address this directly, so read the clause before you sign.

There is one major exception. When the buyer is a first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the house as a principal residence, the seller pays all of the State transfer tax, and also the recordation and local transfer tax unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

Several conditions apply to that rule. Each buyer on the deed must sign a statement under oath, and with two or more buyers every one of them must qualify. The first-time buyer State transfer tax rate is 0.25% rather than 0.5%, which cuts the seller's share of that line.

Recordation tax law also lets a local government exempt an amount for owner-occupied homes when the buyer lives there at least 7 months of a 12 month period. Ask the clerk or your title company whether your county does.

How much do transfer and recordation taxes differ between Maryland counties?

County rates differ a lot, so the same price can produce very different bills. The Department of Legislative Services lists fiscal 2026 rates for each jurisdiction.

CountyRecordation (per $500)County transfer tax
Baltimore County$2.501.5%
Howard$2.501.25%
Harford$3.301.0%
Carroll$6.500.0%
Frederick$7.000.0%

Montgomery County varies by property value and adds a recordation surcharge on transactions over $500,000. Anne Arundel's transfer tax runs from 1.0% to 1.5%. Statewide, recordation runs from $2.50 to $7.00 per $500, and the transfer tax from 0% to 1.5%.

What would the taxes be on a $400,000 Maryland house?

On a $400,000 sale, the State transfer tax is $2,000 in every county, and the county charges change the total. The figures below are our own arithmetic from the published rates, shown as an illustration, not a quote.

LineHarfordHoward
State transfer tax at 0.5%$2,000$2,000
County transfer tax$4,000 (1.0%)$5,000 (1.25%)
Recordation tax$2,640 ($3.30 x 800)$2,000 ($2.50 x 800)
Combined$8,640$9,000

If the buyer and seller split these equally under the default rule, each side carries half. If the buyer qualifies as a first-time Maryland buyer, the State transfer tax falls to 0.25% and the seller covers the full set unless the contract says otherwise.

What recording fees and surcharges does the clerk add?

The Clerk of the Circuit Court charges a recording fee of $20 for most deeds of nine pages or less and a $40 surcharge on nearly every recorded instrument. Both Harford and Howard County list the same figures.

  • Release of nine pages or less: $10.
  • Instrument of ten pages or more that is not a principal residence: $75.
  • Copies: $0.50 a page in Harford County, plus $5 for a certified copy.
  • Harford Land Records e-records through Simplifile.

Recording fees are non-refundable, and State transfer tax refunds need a claim form returned to the clerk. When a tax exemption applies, the document must cite the full exemption code. Without it, the clerk charges full tax.

What property tax steps come before a Maryland deed transfers?

Real Property Article 3-104 requires property taxes, assessments and charges due to be paid, with the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed, before the transfer is entered on the assessment books. A county or municipality may charge up to $55 for a certificate of paid charges in certain counties.

Counties set their own procedure. Harford County sells a Certificate of Tax Liens and Other Charges Due for $50 that is valid 90 days, and county staff stamp every deed before recording. In Howard County, deeds go through the Department of Finance's Division of Recordation Tax before they reach Land Records.

Unpaid tax is the line most likely to surprise a seller. Maryland sells liens at annual tax sales, and an owner can redeem a property by paying the lien, interest and fees any time before a circuit judge signs a foreclosure order.

Where do the county steps happen and how long do they take?

Each county has two stops: a county tax office that collects and stamps, and the Circuit Court land records office that records the deed. Two sample counties show how the hours and timing differ.

  • Harford: Revenue Collections at 220 S. Main Street, Bel Air, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, with processing that usually takes 24 to 48 hours.
  • Harford Land Records: 20 West Courtland Street, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a 4:00 p.m. courier and title company cutoff.
  • Howard: Division of Recordation Tax at 3430 Courthouse Drive, Ellicott City, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Howard Land Records: 9250 Judicial Way, Suite 1900, with recording hours of 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

Harford walk-ins are limited to five documents or sets at a time.

What about sellers who live out of state?

A nonresident individual seller has 8.75% of the total sale payment withheld at settlement, and a nonresident entity has 8.25% withheld. Form MW506NRS reports it, and the deed cannot be recorded without the payment.

The withholding is an advance on income tax, not a closing cost in the normal sense. If you owe less, you can apply for an early refund when the price is below $1.5 million. See our Maryland capital gains guide for the full rules.

How do closing costs work in a direct cash sale?

The same taxes and fees apply to a cash sale as to a financed one, because they are charges on the deed and on the tax account. What changes is who agrees to pay which item in the contract.

Before you sign anything, ask for a written net sheet that lists each tax line. Check three things: whether the buyer claims first-time buyer status, who pays the county transfer tax and recordation tax, and what the county shows as owed on the tax account. Your title company or attorney can confirm each one.

More questions about Maryland Closing Costs for Sellers

Who pays the Maryland transfer tax?

Unless the contract says otherwise, buyer and seller split the State and local transfer taxes and the recordation tax equally. When a first-time Maryland buyer will live in the house, the seller pays all of the State transfer tax and, by default, the local taxes too.

What is the Maryland State transfer tax rate?

It is 0.5% of the consideration. For a first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the house as a principal residence, the rate is 0.25% and the seller pays all of it.

How much is the recordation tax in Maryland?

Each county sets it per $500 of consideration. The legislature's table lists $2.50 in Howard and Baltimore Counties, $3.30 in Harford, and $7.00 in Frederick.

Do Maryland sellers pay a recording fee?

The clerk charges $20 for most deeds of nine pages or less and a $40 surcharge. Whether the buyer or seller covers it depends on the contract.

Is property tax paid before closing in Maryland?

Yes. Taxes, assessments and charges due must be paid, with the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed, before the transfer is entered on the assessment books.

  • Turn the Maryland Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Maryland personal income tax rates start at 2% on the first $1,000 and rise to a maximum of 5.75% (tax year 2021 page). (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Maryland's 23 counties and Baltimore City levy a local income tax collected on the resident state return. (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Nonresidents are subject to a special tax rate of 2.25% in addition to the state income tax rate (tax year 2021 page). (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Nonresident sellers of real property are subject to withholding of 8.75% (individuals) or 8.25% (entities) of the sale payment. (Comptroller: Employer Withholding; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Maryland have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?

Maryland has no separate capital gains rate for most sellers: gain from a house is added to income and taxed at the regular state rates, plus a local income tax. Starting with tax year 2025, an extra 2% applies to net capital gains for people whose federal adjusted gross income is above $350,000.

Before that change, the Comptroller's Technical Bulletin 58 notes, capital gains were taxed at the same rate as ordinary income. The new 2% sits on top of the regular tax, so a seller above the threshold pays both. Corporations are not subject to it. A pass-through entity does not pay it, though an owner who receives a gain from one can, and a trust or estate with federal taxable income over $350,000 owes it on undistributed gains.

Most Maryland homeowners selling a primary residence never meet the surtax, because the bulletin excludes that gain when it applies. The details are in the next sections.

Which Maryland house sales are excluded from the extra 2% tax?

A primary residence that sells for less than $1.5 million is excluded from the 2% surtax. The excluded property types are a single-family home, townhome, row home, or residential condo or co-op unit, including the land and any accessory dwelling unit.

The same bulletin lists several other exclusions that are less relevant to a house seller but worth knowing:

  • Gain held in retirement accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA.
  • Land under a conservation, agricultural or forest preservation easement.
  • Gain deferred in a like-kind exchange under IRC section 1031, because it is not in federal AGI.
  • Affordable housing owned by a nonprofit.

A rental house, a second home or an inherited house that was never your residence does not fit the primary residence description in the bulletin, so for a seller above the $350,000 line the gain on it can be subject to the extra 2%.

What Maryland income tax rates apply to the gain?

Maryland's top brackets for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 are 5.75%, 6.25% and 6.5%, based on income. Lower brackets start at 2% on the first $1,000, per the Comptroller's individual income tax page, which also notes the county and Baltimore City local tax.

State rateSingle filersJoint filers and heads of household
5.75%$250,001 to $500,000$300,001 to $600,000
6.25%$500,001 to $1,000,000$600,001 to $1,200,000
6.50%Over $1,000,000Over $1,200,000

Local income tax is the second layer. Counties may charge up to 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County lists 3.06% and Howard County 3.20% for calendar 2026.

Because a house gain is counted in income, a large gain can push the year's income into a higher bracket. A tax professional can run the numbers for your own return.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for a Maryland seller?

Under IRS Topic 701, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of your main home, or $500,000 if you file jointly. To qualify you must have owned the home at least 24 months and lived in it as your main home at least 24 months during the 5 years ending on the sale date.

The two tests can be met in different 2-year periods. You generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale in the 2 years before this one.

A reduced exclusion may be available when the sale is driven by a work, health or unforeseeable event, such as a death, divorce or a home destroyed by disaster. The IRS formula divides your qualifying time by 730 days and multiplies by $250,000. Report the sale if you receive Form 1099-S or if you cannot exclude all of the gain, using Schedule D and Form 8949.

What federal rates apply when the gain is more than the exclusion?

Gain on a home owned more than one year is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% federally, depending on income. The IRS lists these ceilings for tax years beginning in 2025:

  • 0% up to $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • 15% above that, up to $533,400 for single filers, $600,050 for joint filers and $566,700 for heads of household.
  • 20% above the 15% range.

Gain on a home held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property, which comes from depreciation, is taxed at up to 25%.

The 3.8% net investment income tax can also apply. Its thresholds are $200,000 for single filers and heads of household and $250,000 for joint filers. Gain on a principal residence generally escapes it to the extent the gain is excluded, while gain above the exclusion can count.

How do you work out the gain on a Maryland house?

The gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis. The IRS defines amount realized as the selling price minus selling expenses, and basis starts with what you paid, including purchase costs, then rises with improvements that add value.

Because selling expenses reduce the amount realized, the closing costs you pay at settlement come back into the math. Keep the final settlement statement.

Inherited houses follow a special rule. Your basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date the estate chose. If an estate tax return was filed or required, the value on that return is your basis.

Rental or business use needs care. The IRS says depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded and is recognized as unrecaptured section 1250 gain. Periods after 2008 when the property was not your principal residence are generally nonqualified use, and gain allocated to those periods cannot be excluded.

What does a nonresident seller of Maryland real estate owe at closing?

A nonresident selling Maryland real property must have tax withheld at settlement: 8.75% of the total payment for individuals and 8.25% for entities, for sales after June 30, 2025. The deed cannot be recorded unless the withholding payment accompanies it.

Form MW506NRS reports it. Sellers who owe less, or none, can apply for an early refund when the sale price is below $1.5 million. At $1.5 million or more, no tentative refund is available and the seller files a full annual return, with Form 502CG where it applies. Form MW506AE is the application for a certificate of full or partial exemption.

The withholding does not include the extra 2% surtax. A seller who expects that tax should make additional estimated payments, using Form 502D.

Seller typeWithholding on sales after June 30, 2025
Nonresident individual8.75% of total payment
Nonresident entity8.25% of total payment

Do Maryland taxes change if the buyer pays cash or is an investor?

No. Maryland and federal tax on your gain follow your basis, your holding period and your income, not who buys the house or how the buyer pays. A cash buyer simply means the price you realize is the price in the contract.

What a quick cash sale changes is time. If you want to qualify for the home sale exclusion, check the 24-month tests before you sign, because the date of sale is the date that counts.

Keep the settlement statement, the closing disclosure from your purchase and receipts for improvements. Those documents prove your basis if the IRS or the Comptroller asks.

More questions about Maryland Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Maryland capital gains tax on selling a home?

Maryland taxes the gain as income, with local tax on top, and adds a 2% surtax on net capital gains when federal adjusted gross income is above $350,000. A primary residence that sells for less than $1.5 million is excluded from that surtax.

How much of my home sale gain can I exclude federally?

Up to $250,000 if you file as single, or $500,000 for joint filers. You must have owned the home and used it as your main home for at least 24 months in the 5 years before the sale.

Do Maryland counties add tax to my capital gain?

Yes, through the local income tax, which is capped at 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County lists 3.06% and Howard County 3.20%.

What happens if I live out of state and sell a Maryland house?

Tax is withheld at settlement: 8.75% for a nonresident individual and 8.25% for an entity. You can apply for a refund of the excess if the price is below $1.5 million, and above that you file a full annual return.

What is my tax basis in an inherited Maryland house?

It is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date the estate chose. If an estate tax return was required or filed, the value on it is your basis.

title: Maryland Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale
content:
Maryland Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale

Cash Home Buyers in Maryland
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maryland Tax Sales: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maryland Tax Sales sale
  • Turn the Maryland Tax Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maryland House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The owner may redeem any time until the right of redemption is finally foreclosed (Tax-Property 14-827); the owner keeps possession in the meantime. (SDAT: Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman; source)
  • The certificate states the redemption interest rate: 6% a year or as fixed by the County Commissioners (Anne Arundel example: 1.5% per month, 18% per annum). (SDAT: Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman; source)
  • A final judgment in the foreclosure vests absolute fee simple title in the plaintiff free of prior encumbrances except later taxes and easements. (SDAT: Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman; source)
  • A money judgment is a lien for the judgment amount and post-judgment interest; in counties other than Baltimore City, the creditor must request recording of the lien. (Maryland Courts: Judgments & Debt Collection; source)
  • The county collector's certificate showing taxes and charges paid is required before a deed is recorded and the transfer is made on assessment books. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What happens at a Maryland tax sale?

The county sells a lien, not the house. A buyer at the auction pays the overdue tax bill and receives a tax lien certificate, and the homeowner keeps ownership and possession while the debt is outstanding.

The State Department of Assessments and Taxation runs an Office of the State Tax Sale Ombudsman page that lays out the calendar. Property taxes are due July 1 and overdue October 1. Principal residences can pay in two installments, due September 30 and December 31. A collector must mail a notice at least 30 days before newspaper advertising starts, and the sale is advertised weekly for four weeks.

About six months after the sale, the purchaser receives a certificate of sale, and it is void if no foreclosure case is filed within two years. Counties run their own sales, so dates and minimum amounts differ. Baltimore City, for instance, follows a notice calendar that runs from a February final bill to a sale in the third week of May, with payment due April 30 to stop it, according to People's Law Library.

  • Sold: the lien, through a tax lien certificate.
  • Not sold: the title to the house.
  • Owner keeps: possession and the right to redeem until a court forecloses.

How big is tax sale activity in Maryland?

In 2024, counties mailed final bill and legal notices to 77,050 properties statewide, and 16,205 liens were offered for sale. Most owners who get a notice resolve it before the auction.

The figures below come from SDAT's 2025 annual tax sale report, which covers tax sales held in 2024 and redemptions and foreclosures in fiscal year 2024. Twenty-four jurisdictions, the 23 counties and Baltimore City, supplied data.

MeasureFigure reported
Final bill and legal notices mailed77,050
Liens advertised in the first notice41,784 (average lien $5,399)
Liens offered for sale16,205
Owner-occupied parcels advertised13,669
Owner-occupied parcels offered4,013
Owner-occupied liens sold3,888 (average lien $3,102)
Owner-occupied properties redeemed before foreclosure3,012
Owner-occupied foreclosures by private lien holders81 (average lien $4,948)

The same report says the ombudsman assisted about 10,116 homeowners in fiscal year 2025 and more than 20,000 since 2020. The gap between 13,669 advertised parcels and 81 foreclosures shows how many owners pay, redeem or get help along the way.

What changed on January 1, 2026?

Chapter 231 of the 2025 laws (House Bill 59) tightened tax sale rules for owner-occupied homes, effective January 1, 2026. It applies only to tax sale certificates issued after that date.

  • A home occupied by an heir of a deceased owner is treated like an owner-occupied home, and local governments may withhold it from sale.
  • The mandatory withholding threshold for owner-occupied and heir-occupied homes rises from $750 to $1,000.
  • A property must be withheld when the only tax lien is for unpaid water and sewer charges, statewide.
  • The redemption rate for owner-occupied residential property cannot exceed 10 percent per year.
  • Post-sale taxes, interest and penalties cannot be added to the redemption price for owner-occupied homes.
  • Foreclosure complaints on owner-occupied homes can be filed after 12 months instead of 9, and the first required notice cannot go out until 10 months after the sale.

The law also makes counties and Baltimore City set up a registry where interested parties, or the State Tax Sale Ombudsman, can designate properties to be withheld.

How does redemption work and what does it cost?

The owner pays the certificate holder what is owed and the lien is cleared. The total includes the original tax debt, interest at the rate on the certificate, and allowed fees, and it grows the longer the owner waits.

People's Law Library puts the range at 6 percent to 18 percent a year depending on the county. SDAT gives two examples: Anne Arundel County at 1.5 percent a month, or 18 percent a year, and Baltimore County at 12 percent a year. For owner-occupied homes on certificates issued under the 2026 rules, the cap is 10 percent.

An owner can redeem any time until a court finally forecloses the right of redemption. SDAT adds that some purchaser fees become recoverable after four months, so redeeming in the early weeks costs less. People's Law Library advises asking the Collector of Taxes for the redemption amount in writing and redeeming before final judgment, because paying afterward does not restore the owner's rights.

What does a foreclosure of the right of redemption involve?

The certificate holder must file a case in circuit court after a waiting period, and the owner is entitled to written notice first. If the court enters a final judgment, the holder takes title free of earlier encumbrances other than later taxes and easements.

The waiting period before filing has been six months in most counties and nine months for owner-occupied homes, per SDAT. People's Law Library describes two notices, a pre-foreclosure notice and then a notice of intent sent at least 30 days before the complaint. The holder has to prove both were sent.

Tenants in a foreclosed rental house are covered too. Under the 2025 law, a tenant must get at least 90 days' notice before the plaintiff takes possession, up from 30, and notices must be posted on the property within 5 days instead of 1. Foreclosure plaintiffs on owner-occupied property must also notify the State Tax Sale Ombudsman.

What help exists for owners facing a tax sale?

Maryland offers a state loan program, income-based tax credits and a free help center. Use them early, since options narrow after the sale.

  • Homeowner Protection Program: People's Law Library says it may keep an eligible home out of tax sale for at least 3 years. Listed limits are an assessed value of $300,000 or less, combined income of $60,000 or less, and non-property assets of $200,000 or less, with priority for owners over 60, people on disability benefits and long-time residents.
  • Homeowners' Property Tax Credit: income based, reapplied for yearly, with a September 1 application deadline.
  • Homestead Tax Credit: caps yearly taxable assessment increases and needs a one-time application.
  • Tax Sale Help Center: by appointment at 123 Market Place in Baltimore; call (410) 767-4994 or email sdat.taxsale@maryland.gov.

Owners can also contact the Legal Aid Bureau or the Maryland Volunteer Lawyers Service, both named by People's Law Library, if court papers arrive.

Can I sell my Maryland house before the tax sale?

Yes. Because the owner still holds title until a court says otherwise, a house with a tax lien can be sold, and the unpaid taxes are paid out of the closing proceeds.

Real Property Article 3-104 requires the county collector's certificate showing taxes and charges paid before a deed is recorded, so the debt cannot be skipped at closing. Selling before the auction avoids certificate interest, foreclosure risk and the costs that may be added to a redemption.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including houses behind on property taxes or carrying other liens. If you have a final bill or sale notice, call the collector first for the exact payoff, then compare options with the sale deadline in mind.

SDAT's report lists bid balance funds held by counties, with Baltimore City holding the most at $8,783,544, Prince George's County $8,488,803 and Montgomery County $6,519,562. Ask the county collector what applies to a specific property.

More questions about Maryland Tax Sales

Do I lose my house at a Maryland tax sale?

No, not at the sale. The county sells a tax lien certificate and the homeowner keeps the property. The owner can lose it only if the certificate holder forecloses the right of redemption and a court enters final judgment.

How long do I have to redeem after a Maryland tax sale?

Until a court finally forecloses the right of redemption. Waiting periods before a foreclosure case can be filed run from six months upward, and 12 months for owner-occupied homes under certificates issued from 2026.

What interest do I pay to redeem?

The rate on the certificate, which People's Law Library gives as 6 to 18 percent a year by county. For owner-occupied homes under the 2026 law it cannot exceed 10 percent.

When are Maryland property taxes overdue?

October 1, according to SDAT. They are due July 1, and principal residences may pay in two installments on September 30 and December 31.

Can a home occupied by an heir be sold at tax sale?

Under Chapter 231 of 2025, an heir-occupied residence is treated like an owner-occupied home. Local governments may withhold it from sale, and it must be withheld when taxes owed are under the mandatory threshold.

content:
Maryland Recording a Deed: Fees, Where to File and What to Bring

Cash Home Buyers in Maryland
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maryland Recording a Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maryland Recording a Deed sale
  • Turn the Maryland Recording a Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maryland House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Deeds are recorded with the clerk of the circuit court; the clerk may record a change-of-ownership instrument only with the tax collector's certificate and a complete intake sheet. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
  • A complete intake sheet states the property identifier, parties, instrument type, consideration, recording charges and taxes, claimed exemptions, and tax bill mailing address. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
  • A deed (other than a mortgage or deed of trust) must bear a certification by a Maryland attorney, or by a party named in it, that the instrument was prepared by that person. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
  • Recording requires all public taxes, assessments and charges currently due to be paid and the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
  • A $40 surcharge on recordable instruments continues on and after July 1, 2020 (Chapter 538 of 2020). (Howard County Circuit Court Land Records; source)
  • E-recording is available (Howard County clerk). (Howard County Circuit Court Land Records; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where is a deed recorded in Maryland?

A Maryland deed is recorded in the land records of the county where the property sits, through the Clerk of the Circuit Court for that county.

Counties differ in how the paperwork reaches the clerk. In Harford County, for example, the Land Records Department in Bel Air takes documents three ways: e-recording through Simplifile, mail, or walk-in. Walk-in customers there are limited to five documents or sets at a time, and recorded papers go back by U.S. Mail unless the customer asks otherwise.

Hours matter on closing day. Harford's land records counter runs 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays, with a 4:00 PM cutoff for couriers and title companies. Ask the title company when the deed will actually reach the counter, since a late submission can slow the date a seller is paid.

  • Recording is county based: use the land records of the county where the house is located.
  • Some counties split the work. Baltimore County sends deeds through its Transfer and Recordation Section before the Circuit Court finalizes them.
  • E-recording through a vendor such as Simplifile is one option, and the clerk can give account details.

What must a deed have before the clerk will record it?

The clerk needs a complete intake sheet, proof that taxes are current, and the correct fees and taxes. Without those, the instrument is returned.

Real Property Article 3-104 sets the core rules. A complete intake sheet lists the property identifier, parties, instrument type, consideration, recording charges and taxes, claimed exemptions and the tax bill mailing address. A deed also needs a certification that a Maryland attorney, or a party named in the deed, prepared it. The collector must endorse the deed to show that current taxes and charges are paid.

Baltimore County states the lien certificate rule bluntly on its deed transfer and recordation page: a deed that changes ownership and arrives without a lien certificate will not be processed. The same page says agricultural-use deeds and partial transfer deeds need approval from the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation first, at its Towson office.

Sellers can catch most delays before closing by asking the title company three questions.

  • Is the lien certificate ordered, and does it show any unpaid county or municipal charges?
  • Who prepared the deed, and is the preparer certification signed?
  • Does the intake sheet name the right exemption code, if any is claimed?

What does it cost to record a deed in Maryland?

Recording a deed costs a per-document fee plus a flat surcharge, and the taxes are billed on top. The clerk's fee depends mainly on page count and on whether the property is a principal residence.

The Cecil County clerk's recording fee schedule and the Harford County page show the same structure. The table gives the figures both pages list.

ItemAmount listed
Release, 9 pages or fewer$10.00
Other instrument, 9 pages or fewer, or principal residence only$20.00
Other instrument, 10 pages or more$75.00
Surcharge on most recordable instruments$40.00
State transfer tax (Cecil and Harford pages)0.50% of consideration
State transfer tax, first-time Maryland buyer, principal residence0.25%

Harford adds that recording fees are non-refundable, while a state transfer tax refund needs a claim form filed with the clerk. Copies cost $0.50 a page there, and certification costs $5.00. Check the page count of the deed, because it decides which tier applies.

How do recordation and transfer taxes vary by county?

The state transfer tax is the same everywhere, but recordation tax and county transfer tax change from one county to the next. Always get the county's own figure from the title company or the county revenue office.

Two county pages show the spread. Baltimore County lists a county transfer tax of 1.5 percent of consideration and a state recordation tax of $2.50 for each $500 or fraction of consideration. Cecil County's clerk lists recordation tax at $4.10 per $500, rounded, of the actual consideration. In Harford County, county transfer tax and recordation tax are collected by the county's Revenue Collections office on South Main Street in Bel Air, and the clerk collects the recording fees and state transfer tax.

That split affects how a closing is funded. Checks may be payable to the Clerk of the Circuit Court, to the county government, or to both, depending on the county. A seller who is paying transfer tax out of proceeds should see a line-by-line estimate before signing.

  • Baltimore County: payments go to Baltimore County, Maryland, at the Office of Budget and Finance in Towson.
  • Harford County: county taxes go to Harford County Revenue, fees to the Clerk.
  • Cecil County: fees are paid at the Department of Finance.

Which exemptions can lower the tax bill?

Maryland law lets counties exempt first-time buyers of owner-occupied homes from part of the tax, and it exempts some family and estate transfers entirely. Exemptions must be claimed on the intake sheet, and Harford warns that a claimed exemption must cite the full exemption code or the full tax is charged.

Under Tax-Property Article 12-103(b), a county or Baltimore City may adopt a recordation tax exemption on a set amount of consideration for owner-occupied residential property, if the buyer will occupy the home for at least 7 months of a 12-month period. A second option covers a person who has never owned a Maryland principal residence and will occupy the property, and each grantee signs a sworn statement. For the state transfer tax, Cecil's page describes the first-time buyer rate of 0.25 percent and the sworn statement from each grantee.

Transfers under Maryland's new transfer-on-death deed law are also exempt from state recordation tax, state transfer tax and county transfer tax when the property is the transferor's primary or secondary residence, according to Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws. Heirs may still owe inheritance tax.

What do sellers and heirs run into when a deed is recorded?

The recurring problems are missing lien certificates, unpaid taxes, a wrong legal description and an unrecorded prior deed in the chain of title. Each one stops the clerk, or the title company, from closing.

Estate sales add steps, because the intake sheet must name the parties and the instrument type correctly, and the preparer certification still applies to the deed.

Transfers of an entity that owns real estate can also be taxed as if a deed were recorded. The Maryland Association of Counties explains in a December 2025 roadmap that moving more than 80 percent of the equity in an entity that owns real property can trigger recordation tax under Tax-Property 12-117, with transfer tax extended by 13-103. Owners who hold a rental house in an LLC should check this before selling membership interests.

Nonresident sellers have one more item. Harford's page notes that Maryland Comptroller withholding on real property sales by nonresidents may apply and is collected by the Clerk.

  • Confirm the legal description matches the last recorded deed.
  • Pay or payoff any county water, sewer or tax charges before the lien certificate is ordered.
  • Ask whether an exemption applies and gather the sworn statements early.
  • For an inherited house, confirm who has authority to sign before the deed is drafted.

How does selling a house for cash change the recording step?

A cash sale uses the same recording steps, with fewer moving parts. With no lender, there is no new deed of trust to record beside the deed, and the file usually closes once the title company confirms the lien certificate and taxes.

A seller still signs a deed, and the clerk still receives the intake sheet and collects the fees. Cash Home Buyers can buy houses in Maryland as-is, including homes with open liens or title questions that need to be cleared at closing. Because the deed has to be recorded to complete the transfer, ask the title company when the recording is scheduled and who is paying each tax line.

More questions about Maryland Recording a Deed

Where do I record a deed in Maryland?

With the Clerk of the Circuit Court in the county where the property is located. Many counties accept e-recording, mail and walk-in filing, and some route deeds through a county revenue office first.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Maryland?

The clerk's fee is $20 for most deeds of nine pages or fewer and $75 for ten pages or more, plus a $40 surcharge, according to the Cecil and Harford clerk pages. Transfer and recordation taxes are charged separately and vary by county.

What is the Maryland state transfer tax rate?

The state rate listed on the Cecil and Harford pages is 0.50 percent of the consideration, or 0.25 percent for a first-time Maryland buyer who will use the home as a principal residence. Sworn statements are required for the lower rate.

Can a deed be recorded without a lien certificate?

Generally no. Real Property Article 3-104 requires the collector's certificate for a change-of-ownership instrument, and Baltimore County says a deed without a lien certificate will not be processed.

Does a transfer-on-death deed need to be recorded?

Yes. Under Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws, a transfer-on-death deed is effective only if it is recorded in the county land records before the owner dies.
